lead: A biosensor is named twice: once by the biological element that recognises the target, and once by the transducer that turns that recognition into a signal. Enzyme with an amperometric electrode gives the glucose strip. Antibody with an optical surface gives the surface plasmon resonance immunosensor. DNA with a field-effect transistor gives the GenFET. The three cases exams ask for are the ISFET, the IMFET and the glucose sensor. Learn the naming rule and you can predict the design of an unfamiliar sensor before you see its circuit.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for the biosensor block diagram, Chapter 5.4 for the FET as a transducer, and Unit 1 for sensitivity, selectivity and drift.

sections.h3: Two axes give every biosensor its name

blocks.text: A biosensor has two parts in series: a biological element that recognises one molecule, and a transducer that converts that recognition into a voltage, a current or a light level. Naming follows the same order. Say the element, say the transducer, and the design is fixed. Enzyme + amperometric = glucose sensor. Antibody + optical = surface plasmon resonance immunosensor. DNA + FET = GenFET.
The element sets the selectivity. Four families cover most work.

items: Enzyme: catalyses one reaction and survives many cycles, so it is reusable and fast. Examples are glucose oxidase, urease, penicillinase.
Antibody: grips one antigen tightly. Very selective, but usually single-use because the binding is hard to reverse.
DNA or aptamer: a DNA strand pairs with its complement; an aptamer is a short strand folded to hold a small molecule.
Whole cell: a bacterium or a tissue slice, used when the target is a mixture, as in BOD and toxicity tests.

blocks.text: The transducer sets the signal. Electrochemical types split three ways: amperometric holds the potential fixed and measures current, potentiometric draws no current and measures EMF, conductometric measures the change in solution conductance. Optical, acoustic (see Chapter 5.9), calorimetric and FET types complete the list.

Start with an n-channel MOSFET. Remove the metal gate and leave the gate oxide bare, touching the electrolyte. That is an ISFET, an ion-sensitive field-effect transistor. A Ag/AgCl reference electrode dips into the solution and sets the gate bias, because a liquid cannot act as a gate on its own.

The bare oxide carries silanol groups. Si–OH ⇌ Si–O⁻ + H⁺, and Si–OH + H⁺ ⇌ Si–OH₂⁺. At high pH the surface loses protons, becomes negative, and pushes electrons out of the channel below. The threshold voltage rises, and at a fixed gate bias the drain current falls because the overdrive V_GS − V_T shrinks.

blocks.where: ΔV_T is the change in threshold voltage in volts; k is Boltzmann's constant 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K; T is absolute temperature in kelvin; q is the electron charge 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; ΔpH is the change in pH. The 59 mV per pH unit is the Nernstian slope.

blocks.text: Two errors dominate. Drift: the reading creeps over hours as the oxide hydrates, so the device needs frequent recalibration. Hysteresis: the reading depends on whether the previous sample was acid or alkali, so the measuring sequence must be fixed.

IMFET. An antibody or an antigen is immobilised on the gate. Binding adds charge to the surface and shifts the threshold, so the device is label-free and needs no fluorescent tag. The weakness is ionic strength: counter-ions in a salty buffer screen the bound charge within about a nanometre, so only binding right at the surface is seen.

EnFET. An enzyme layer sits over the ISFET gate and the local pH change reports the substrate. Urease on urea releases ammonia and the local pH rises; penicillinase on penicillin releases acid and the local pH falls. The initial rate of pH change gives the concentration. Biology makes a chemical, and the transistor reads the chemical.

Glucose oxidase (GOx) is the enzyme. It carries an FAD cofactor and catalyses the reaction below. Glucose is oxidised, oxygen is the electron acceptor, and hydrogen peroxide is the product the electrode sees.
glucose + O₂ → gluconolactone + H₂O₂ (catalysed by GOx)
blocks.where: glucose is the blood sugar being measured; O₂ is dissolved oxygen; gluconolactone is the oxidised product; H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, the electroactive species.

blocks.text: First generation. The H₂O₂ is oxidised at a platinum electrode held at about +0.6 to +0.7 V against Ag/AgCl. Each glucose molecule hands over two electrons, so the current is proportional to the glucose reaching the enzyme. The flaw is the high potential: ascorbic acid, uric acid and paracetamol in blood also oxidise near +0.7 V and add a false current.
Q = n_e F,  I = Q / t
blocks.where: Q is charge in coulombs; n_e is the moles of electrons released, twice the moles of glucose; F = 96 485 C/mol is the Faraday constant; I is the average current in amperes; t is the time in seconds.

blocks.text: Second generation. A mediator such as ferrocene or ferricyanide carries electrons from the enzyme's FAD to the electrode, so the electrode can run at about +0.2 to +0.4 V. Fewer interferents oxidise there, and dissolved oxygen no longer competes with the mediator.

items: Disposable strip: 5 to 10 µL of finger-prick blood fills a capillary, a fixed potential is applied for about 5 s, and the charge gives the glucose. One use, then discard.
Continuous subcutaneous monitor: a small needle sits in interstitial fluid and reports every few minutes for days, with an occasional finger-prick check.

blocks.text: Normal fasting blood glucose is about 4 to 7 mmol/L, that is 72 to 126 mg/dL using 1 mmol/L = 18 mg/dL. Clinical cut-offs for diabetes belong to a medical text, not to a sensor course.

figure.caption: Every biosensor sits where the biological-element axis meets the transducer axis. The FET branch, the one this chapter follows, splits into the ISFET, the IMFET and the enzyme FET (EnFET).

spec.aria: A two-axis tree naming a biosensor by its biological element and by its transducer, with the FET branch splitting into ISFET, IMFET and enzyme FET.

examples.question: A disposable glucose strip is filled with 10 µL of blood whose glucose concentration is 5.5 mmol/L. Each glucose molecule releases 2 electrons at the platinum electrode. The enzyme reaction goes to completion in 10 s. Find (a) the moles of glucose, (b) the moles of electrons, (c) the total charge and (d) the average current. Take F = 96 485 C/mol.
steps: Convert the volume to litres: 10 µL = 10 × 10⁻⁶ L = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ L.
Moles of glucose: n_g = c × V = 5.5 × 10⁻³ mol/L × 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ L = 5.5 × 10⁻⁸ mol.
Moles of electrons: n_e = 2 × n_g = 2 × 5.5 × 10⁻⁸ = 1.1 × 10⁻⁷ mol.
Average current: I = Q / t = 1.061 × 10⁻² C / 10 s = 1.061 × 10⁻³ A = 1.06 mA.
examples.answer: The strip passes 10.6 mC of charge, which is an average current of about 1.06 mA over the 10 s.
examples.check:
c = 5.5e-3
V = 10e-6
F = 96485
t = 10
n_g = c * V
n_e = 2 * n_g
Q = n_e * F
I = Q / t
print(n_g)
print(n_e)
print(Q)
print(I)

traps: Reversing the ISFET sign. For an n-channel device at a fixed gate bias the output falls as pH rises, because the threshold voltage rises and the overdrive shrinks.
Forgetting the 2 electrons per glucose molecule, or using the moles of glucose directly in Q = nF. The factor of two comes from H₂O₂ oxidation at platinum.
Mixing up volts and millivolts in the 59 mV/pH slope, or feeding a pH difference in the wrong units into ΔV_T.
Calling a bare ISFET a biosensor. It is a chemical pH sensor; it becomes a biosensor only when an enzyme or antibody layer is added, giving the EnFET or the IMFET.
Swapping IMFET and EnFET. The IMFET carries an antibody or antigen on the gate; the EnFET carries an enzyme that changes the local pH.
Using µL and mol/L together without converting the volume to litres first.

quiz.q: Name the biological element and the transducer in a disposable glucose strip.
quiz.a: Glucose oxidase, an enzyme, and a platinum amperometric electrode that oxidises the hydrogen peroxide produced.

quiz.q: What physical change turns a MOSFET into an ISFET?
quiz.a: The metal gate is removed and the gate oxide is left exposed to the electrolyte; a reference electrode supplies the gate bias.

quiz.q: Why does an ISFET need a reference electrode when the solution already touches the gate oxide?
quiz.a: A liquid has no fixed potential of its own. The Ag/AgCl reference closes the circuit and defines the gate-to-source voltage, so a pH reading means something and can be repeated.

quiz.q: For an n-channel ISFET at fixed gate bias, explain why the drain current falls when pH rises.
quiz.a: Si–OH groups lose protons, the surface charge becomes more negative, the threshold voltage rises, the overdrive V_GS − V_T falls, and the drain current falls with it.

quiz.q: An n-channel ISFET at 25 °C reads pH 7.00 and then pH 7.40. Using 59 mV/pH, find the change in threshold voltage and state the direction of the current change.
quiz.a: ΔV_T = 59 mV/pH × 0.40 pH = 23.6 mV. The threshold rises, so at fixed gate bias the drain current falls.

quiz.q: An IMFET gives a strong signal in dilute buffer but almost none in a high-salt buffer at the same antigen concentration. Explain.
quiz.a: Ionic screening. Counter-ions in the electrolyte shield the charge of the bound antigen within about a nanometre, the Debye length, so the gate never feels the binding charge. Lowering the ionic strength widens the screening length and the signal returns.

quiz.q: Why does a ferrocene mediator reduce interference in a glucose sensor?
quiz.a: Ferrocene carries electrons from the enzyme's FAD to the electrode at about +0.2 to +0.4 V. Hydrogen peroxide needs +0.6 to +0.7 V. Ascorbate, urate and paracetamol oxidise at the higher potential, so running lower removes most of their false current. The mediator also removes the dependence on dissolved oxygen.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wearable microneedle patches now read interstitial glucose without a finger prick, and graphene and silicon-nanowire FET arrays push label-free detection towards single molecules. CRISPR-Cas systems are being used as the recognition element with an electrochemical readout, which turns the two-axis naming rule into a third axis: the molecular machinery. Continuous monitors are being closed into a loop with insulin pumps. Search next for Debye length in FET biosensors, second generation glucose sensors and aptamer-based FET sensors.
